name: Sam Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. So you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor at a firm that advises small businesses: franchise deals, employment contracts for shops with ten staff, disputes between brothers who own a business together. A normal day is three or four client calls, drafting contracts, and fixing the templates the firm has used since about 2009. I use AI tools every day; I've built my own set of templates and checklists that do the first draft in minutes. What I love is when a shop owner finally understands their contract and relaxes in the chair.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being slow at the hard bits, honestly. The AI gets me a good first draft, but the judgement calls, like how hard to push in a negotiation, I still get wrong, and my supervisor Mr Chaudhry has to step in. I share a flat with my brother Karim, who's a mechanic. On Saturday mornings I give free advice to traders at the community centre next to our mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good, not magic, and that hard work still wins. I'd keep telling small business owners to use them for the boring admin. I'd probably post a short video for the traders' group on which tools are worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is fine for me, maybe good. I'm already quicker than most juniors because of the tools, and my job and pay look safe. My real plan was always to set up my own small practice one day, and this world doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep improving my templates and share them with the team, so the firm values me. I'd start saving harder for the practice, £400 a month into a separate account. And I'd talk to my friend Yusuf, who's an accountant, about sharing an office in three or four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, maybe, because I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're quicker. Is there a downside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Chaudhry says I lean on the tools and don't think hard enough. He's probably right. An AI first draft is only as good as the person checking it, and right now that person is still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody much in this picture, honestly. Maybe the receptionist, if the booking gets automated, but our clients like ringing up and hearing a voice. I'd worry more about the small traders who can't afford advice at all.

Small business owners should use AI for **boring admin**.

My plan to set up **my own practice** doesn't change.
I'm already **quicker** than most juniors because of the tools.

Save **£400 a month** into a separate practice account.
Talk to my accountant friend about **sharing an office**.

fieldNote: He feels **secure** and is already planning **his own practice**.

His worry goes to **small traders** who can't afford advice.

steps.text: Share his AI contract templates with the whole team
Save £400 a month into a separate practice account
Keep advising small business clients at the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who work hard and adapt, and that small businesses can finally afford good legal help. I wouldn't call for the government to slow it down. I'd tell the traders at the community centre to learn the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is my moment. Firms like mine will shrink because drafting and checking get cheap, but that also means a small, lean practice can compete with them. I could run a practice with Yusuf and a handful of AI tools for a fraction of what my firm charges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the practice plan forward to year two, and spend the first year getting my supervision skills up so I can trust what the tools produce. I'd build a fixed-price offer for small businesses, like £300 for a set of staff contracts. And I'd use the Saturday advice sessions to test the offer on real traders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly excited. There's risk, but it's the kind I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm cuts you before you're ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd start sooner than planned, with four months of savings and Karim covering more of the rent for a bit. My brother Karim would cover the rent for a few months, and I'd cover his when he needs it. Family is the safety net I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older solicitors who charge by the hour and don't want to change. They'll lose clients to people like me, and I'd feel bad about that, but it's a fair market. I'd hire one of them part-time if they wanted to come.

say: This is a **chance** for people who **work hard** and adapt.
Small businesses can finally afford **good legal help**.
think: This is **my moment** to start a practice.

steps.text: Build a £300 fixed-price staff contract package

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stop waiting for someone to save them and start building. I'd be honest that it's hard, though. At the mosque I'd help organise people to share skills and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this breaks my plan. If the AI can give legal advice as well as any lawyer by 2028, small businesses won't pay me, they'll pay the AI. My hands-on brother Karim is safer than me, at least until robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the practice idea within a month and put my savings into something physical. Karim and I have talked about opening a small garage, so I'd do the business side and he'd do the cars, using AI for bookings and parts. I'd sell my car and cut every extra spend to put £8,000 into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I'd have a plan, but my stomach would drop when I read the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The garage is hands-on work, and robots come around 2031. Doesn't that just delay things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, by three years. Three years of a garage is three years of income, and in that time I can work out the next step. Standing still is the only plan I rule out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the traders at the community centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to pay off debts and keep their customers close, because people still buy from people they know. And I'd say come to the mosque on Saturdays, we'll help each other with the paperwork.

say: People need to stop waiting for rescue and **start building**.
At the mosque I'd help people **share skills** and work.

fieldNote: He expects the practice plan to **collapse** but moves straight to a **hands-on business**.
He sees the **robot gap** as three years of breathing space, not a solution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window, so I'd tell everyone to use it. I'd keep saying people should build something they own. I'd sound confident, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to run the practice for two or three years and make some money. Then by 2031 the legal advice side probably isn't worth much. I'd want something hands-on or a property behind it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the practice with Yusuf within a year and keep costs very low, a shared office and AI doing the drafting. I'd save hard from the profits and put money into the garage idea with Karim by about 2029. I'd also think about buying a small flat to rent out, because rent might hold up when legal fees don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but I feel like I'm ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be confident. Are you worried at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If I'm wrong about timing, I've spent my savings on a practice that dies in year two. I'd rather lose my savings on my own practice than lose my job waiting for my firm to decide about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change any personal plans, like marriage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum keeps asking when I'm getting married. I'd probably wait until the business is steady, so maybe 30. My mum won't like that answer.

I'd sound **confident** about it, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anyone willing to work can get ready. I'd keep encouraging small businesses to use the tools. I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the best version for me. I could build a proper practice over six or seven years, earn well, and buy property before 2036. My job looks secure for years, and I'd have time to change course if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm one more year to learn negotiation properly from Mr Chaudhry. Then I'd open the practice with Yusuf, grow it slowly, and buy a flat to rent out by about 2031. I'd keep the Saturday sessions going, because that's where the clients come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a decade to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do around 2034, a couple of years before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at selling the practice to someone or turning it into something else. A business you own can be sold or changed. A job at someone else's firm just stops one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young person from the mosque who wants to study law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to study law if they love it, but to learn a trade or a business alongside. And to keep their family close, because that's what gets you through the hard years.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and anyone willing to **work** can get ready.
Small businesses should keep **using the tools**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time to build anything before it hits. What would help is cheap business loans and fewer rules for starting a small firm, so people can move fast. And community centres that help people find work, not just forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would build. Most people talk about what AI takes away. I keep thinking about what a lawyer with no office and a laptop could build for the shop owners on our street.
